On this page

What is Mosaic ​

Mosaic is a file format for incremental collaboration on geometric, structured data. Many data sources may be combined to form a bigger composed picture, but in the composition they retain their identity and lineage.

It takes lessons from, and addresses shortcomings of, modern data patterns from USD, ECS, JSON and glTF, and combines them into a single flexible data system. Mosaic:

  • is unopinionated on your data
  • can serialize & validate any data type with JSON Schema component schemas
  • allows people to collaborate on that data through file exchange or API
  • takes an ECS approach to decoupling data from use cases
  • elevates parent-child relationships to allow for geometric assembly reuse
  • supports semantic typing through native inheritance

In one paragraph ​

A Mosaic file is a list of sections, each a layer of edits with its author, time and reason. Each section adds or changes nodes, which are ids carrying components: typed values described by JSON Schema, such as a name, a transform, a mesh or a property set. A file can import other files, and its sections layer over theirs. So a model is never one big snapshot. It is many small, owned pieces, composed when you look at them, each still saying where it came from.

Read on for why Mosaic exists and who it is for, or jump to the format, by example.

Status

Mosaic is pre-1.0 and in active development. Expect breaking changes to both the schema and the generated code layout.

The repository ​

This repository holds the format's specification and the tooling used to work with it:

  • src — the format definition, written in TypeSpec, which emits the canonical JSON Schema.
  • standard — the emitted JSON Schema, checked in so consumers can use it without running the toolchain.
  • sdk — runtime libraries (in progress), the mosaic CLI, and sdk/scenarios, where what a user actually does is written in prose and the test beside it is generated from that.

How these relate, and which of them is the standard, is described in The standard and its implementations.
